items.body: China And St. Augustine - Gavekal Research China And St. Augustine Louis-Vincent Gave Gavekal Research | 23 Oct 2026 Back in the summer of 2015, the Chinese government decided that equity markets had risen too far, too fast. The rug was pulled from under margin lending and various restrictions were put in place that brought the unfolding raging equity bull market to an abrupt end. By January 2024, the Chinese government reversed course and decided that Chinese equity prices had fallen far enough. Beijing intervened in the market (see Chinese Policies And Chinese Equities ) and put a floor under domestic markets. Equities duly rallied, delivering very solid returns for 2024 and 2025. However, over the past year, Chinese equity market returns have been fairly dismal. In fact, Chinese equity markets have now fallen for 10 consecutive weeks, a feat they had never achieved before. This in spite of the fact that (a) excitement over all things “artificial intelligence” has been a key driver of global equity market performance and that (b) China is one of the few countries outside of the US actually registering notable gains on the AI front. I was in San Francisco last week to talk to NYU Stern Alumni on October 15, and it was the day that Anthropic had a pre-IPO meeting with prospective investors. While I was not at the meeting, the focus of teh gathering was laying a foundation for its upcoming IPO, with the company reporting third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion, which news reports described as surging 45% over the previous quarter's revenues, and positive profits, albeit on an adjusted basis. During the meeting, Anthropic also reported an annual revenue run rate (ARR) of $67 billion, a metric that those in the AI space have adopted with gusto, with an estimate that the ARR would exceed $100 billion by the end of the year. items.summary_en: A closer look at the impact of China’s currency on China’s export growth.
items.body: Council on Foreign Relations Articles By experts and staff Updated October 11, 2026 12:00 a.m. Brad W. Setser CFR Expert Whitney Shepardson Senior Fellow There is an argument—made in the recent Geneva Report and by various former IMF officials —that China’s current export surge is the simple consequence of the housing downturn and the resulting weakness in Chinese internal demand.* The weakness in the RMB in this story is entirely incidental to the increase in exports, which is, more or less, a mechanical response to weak internal demand. Cannot sell excavators at home? Export them. Built more modern car capacity than your internal market supports ? Export that too… The fall in the nominal RMB over the course of 2022 and the first half of 2023 in nominal and read terms was simply a function of domestic macroeconomic weakness, and a growing rate differential. It wasn’t an active policy choice by China’s central bank. Now, some might note that China’s currency doesn’t always move with rate differentials. items.author: Brad Setser
items.title_en: De-reservification, Not De-dollarization | Council on Foreign Relations
items.summary_en: The world isn’t moving away from the dollar. It is shifting its dollars from traditional reserves to state banks, pension funds, and other quasi-sovereign investors.
items.body: Council on Foreign Relations By experts and staff Published September 15, 2026 8:37 a.m. Brad W. Setser CFR Expert Whitney Shepardson Senior Fellow This is a joint blog with Alex Etra , Senior Macro Strategist and head of Flow of Funds at Vanda Research . The IMF’s data on the currency composition of foreign exchange (FX) reserves is scrutinized carefully for any signs that the world is shifting way from the dollar. Yet it doesn’t really matter that much if the dollar’s share of reserves has shifted from 56.5 percent to 57 percent. The ink-to-impact ratio of the quarterly reporting on the latest COFER data is all off. Neither the stock of global reserves nor the stock of dollar reserves has changed much in the last ten years. The action is elsewhere. China’s state banks (per the Bank of International Settlements) have almost as many foreign assets as the central bank (PBOC). Japan’s Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF) has almost as many foreign assets ( $986 billion ) as the government has FX reserves ($1.1 trillion at the end of August). items.author: Rhodium Group
items.title_en: As Europe Dithers, the Cost of Derisking from China Rises
items.summary_en: The cost of confronting China will be high. But the cost of waiting—for Europe’s economy, security, and sovereignty—could be far higher.
items.body: In March 2023, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called on Europe to unite behind a policy of economic derisking from China. In a speech in Brussels, she warned about Europe’s deepening dependencies on Chinese rare earths, called for more robust trade measures to protect European industry from unfair competition and for new tools to restrict the flow of sensitive technologies to China. More than two and a half years later, it is clear that her warning has gone largely unheeded. Today, Europe is more dependent on critical inputs from China than ever before. China’s export restrictions on critical minerals and chips produced by the Chinese-owned Dutch firm Nexperia have hit European companies in the auto, medical, and defense sectors in recent months, laying bare Europe’s failure to derisk. EU trade defense instruments cover less than 10% of imports from China despite evidence of systemic state support for Chinese companies and an economic model that has relied for years on flooding global markets with cheap goods . Efforts to restrict the flow of artificial intelligence, quantum, and chip technologies to China have stalled amid resistance from European member states

items.summary_en: A blog about markets, finance and all things money related.
items.body: Musings on Markets: Aging in Dog Years? The Short, Glorious Life of a Successful Tech Company! Wednesday, December 9, 2015 Aging in Dog Years? The Short, Glorious Life of a Successful Tech Company! The corporate aging theme is one that I have returned to repeatedly in my posts, and I have looked at how the aging process creates dysfunctional responses on the parts of managers, who want to find ways to reverse it, and investors, who make bets on such reversals. It was the under pinning for my last post on Yahoo , and in that post, I argued that technology companies have compressed life cycles, i.e., age in dog years, relative to non-tech companies. In this post, I would like to provide a rationale for why this may be the case and set the stage for my next post on what the implications are for managers and investors. The Corporate Life Cycle The corporate life cycle follows a familiar pattern. It begins with an idea, that develops into a product, which evolves into an operating business, that matures, and eventually dies. I have also highlighted the transitions that determine whether a company moves to the next stage and the mortality rate especially early in the life cycle is high.

news_items.title_en: In China’s tough job market, anxious students spend thousands on internships | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Facing high youth unemployment and fierce competition for entry-level roles, some students are going all out to secure internships.
news_items.body: Accounting undergraduate student Wang Guilin faces a choice in her search for a winter internship: compete with thousands of applicants through standard recruitment channels or fork out thousands of yuan for a guaranteed placement. Wang considers her academic record average and, to improve her employment prospects after graduation, the second-year student hopes to add experience at a well-known company to her résumé. Yet even internships have become difficult to secure in China’s crowded graduate labour market, forcing many students to turn to brokers to land a spot at the country’s leading firms. “These positions usually go to third- or fourth-year students from top-tier universities or those with strong internship records,” Wang said. “Someone in my position would consider paying for referrals to secure a place.” The services available on the market vary widely. Some agencies offer career coaching, including résumé revisions and interview preparation, while others literally sell guaranteed back-door placements. They do share one thing in common, though: hefty fees. Wang has been quoted between 6,000 yuan (about US$900) and 12,000 yuan for a winter internship at a major accounting

news_items.title_en: Sri Lanka’s property boom gives Chinese developers hope. But familiar risks linger | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Colombo’s luxury property rally is drawing fresh interest from Chinese-backed developments, but analysts warn against speculative excess.
news_items.body: A Chinese developer behind one of Sri Lanka’s biggest projects has reason to celebrate as a luxury property boom lifts sentiment in the South Asian nation and fuels optimism about the market’s prospects. Analysts, however, cautioned that a string of disappointing Chinese overseas property investments over the past decade underlined the risks of speculative excess that could lead to a boom-to-bust scenario, particularly in a country where regulation remained uneven. “Chinese developers, having already learned a hard lesson from the property market [slump in China], need to stay cautious,” said Wang Feng, chairman of Shanghai-based financial services group Ye Lang Capital. “I bet they won’t get carried away by the recent price surge in Sri Lanka because of their high risk-awareness.” Three new luxury residential projects in Colombo Port City – a landmark development built on reclaimed land by China Harbour Engineering Co (Chec) and the Sri Lankan government – had drawn strong interest from local buyers attracted by projections of substantial investment returns, according to a report by online magazine The Diplomat. news_items.title_en: Fandom vs flag: why young Chinese embrace Japanese pop culture but reject war-era symbols | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: For many on the mainland, the recent rising sun flag incident and controversies like it show a fondness for anime and manga only goes so far.
news_items.body: Young Chinese people enjoy Japanese pop culture such as anime and music, but many draw a firm line at symbols of Japanese militarism. That line was tested recently at Moscow State University, where Chinese students confronted a classmate wearing Japan’s rising sun flag in class and called for his repatriation, state-run newspaper Global Times reported on Sunday. Many countries, including China, view the flag as a symbol of Japanese militarism and aggression. Japan’s Self-Defence Forces still use the flag today. The October 14 incident sparked an online backlash against the Chinese student and praise for those who reported him, following commentaries by People’s Daily, the Communist Party’s official newspaper, and the People’s Liberation Army. “A disgrace to the Chinese people,” read one of the top comments under a post by Jun Zhengping, a social media account run by the PLA. Among those condemning the student were people who enjoyed Japanese pop culture, including Lucy Huang, 24.
